To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ethnic minorities' preferences for social interactions can lead to multiple equilibria in urban structures and to adverse labor-market conditions.
ethnic preferences can lead blacks to be segregated in urban neighborhoods and to have worse labor-market outcomes than whites.
ethnic minorities are more likely to be unemployed because of the ethnic preferences of the majority, which leads to the formation of multiple equilibria in the labor market.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: how can ethnic minorities be disadvantaged in the urban labor market, even though they have similar human capital and skills as the majority group?
how social interactions affect the spatial organization of the economy and how this, in turn, can lead to different outcomes in the labor market for different ethnic groups.
how the structure of the labor market affects the outcomes of different racial groups and how these outcomes in turn influence the evolution of the structure of the market.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the US, ethnic minorities are not only discriminated against, they are also discriminated against by themselves, which leads to adverse labor-market and urban outcomes.
the ethnic minorities' labor-market outcomes are worse because of their ethnic preferences.
the labor-market outcomes observed among ethnic minorities are a result of the interaction between their ethnic preferences and the spatial structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ethnic composition of a neighborhood affects its unemployment rates, but the effects differ across groups.
ethnic minorities are not only victims of their own preferences but also of the structure of the urban environment.
ethnic minorities face a double burden in the US: they have to face the negative effects of ethnic preferences as well as the effects of distance to jobs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial concentration of ethnic minorities is an important determinant of their employment outcomes.
the labor-market outcomes observed for ethnic minorities in the US are consistent with a model in which they are discriminated against by whites because of their ethnicity.
ethnic minorities' preferences can lead to the persistence of urban structures and, in the long run, to a persistent disadvantage in the labor market for ethnic minorities.
